Iterative methods extend the range of electromagnetic scattering problems treatable by numerical solutions of integral equations.
Integral equations for electromagnetic scattering often produce dense, non-sparse matrices.
Discretization procedures that preserve convolutional structure lead to Toeplitz or block Toeplitz matrices.
Toeplitz matrices allow storage reduction and efficient computation using FFT.
The method of moments (MOM) approximates unknown functions by basis expansions and testing functions to form matrix equations.
Simple iterative algorithms like Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel can diverge or converge slowly for electromagnetic scattering matrices.
The conjugate gradient method (CGM) is a more robust iterative algorithm that guarantees convergence in finite steps.
FFT reduces the computational complexity of matrix-vector products from O(N²) to O(N log N).
The Discrete-Convolutional Method of Moments (DCMOM) works primarily in the spatial domain and preserves convolutional structure.
The Spectral-Iterative Technique (SIT) samples the kernel's Fourier transform and uses FFT explicitly, often preferred for periodic structures.
Zero-padding in FFT-based methods is used to avoid aliasing but increases computational load; SIT reduces zero-padding requirements.
Electrically large scatterers produce matrix orders exceeding thousands, challenging fast-access memory limits.
Iterative methods do not require explicit storage of the full N×N matrix, reducing memory demands.
Preconditioning techniques can accelerate convergence of iterative algorithms.

Discrete convolutional symmetries are central to reducing storage and computational complexity in these problems.
Periodic structures require special discretization approaches to handle infinite arrays.
The paper discusses the trade-offs between computational efficiency and storage in iterative electromagnetic scattering solutions.
